extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of political/polemical essays; students of rhetoric and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing forceful political/polemical prose that argues against revolutionary measures (esp. confiscation, abolition of institutions) using moral appeals, historical analogy, economic facts, and exposure of hypocrisy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for property; oppose confiscation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confiscate the goods of a single unoffending citizen; sequestration of property without accusation or trial is tyrannical and cruel (e.g., 'Who but a tyrant ... could think of seizing on the property of men, unaccused, unheard, untried').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that proscription and wholesale seizure degrade and impoverish people, turning independence into alms and infamy — a punishment 'worse than death' for many. Use vivid examples of victims (aged clergy, established households) to show moral and social cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test reformers' sincerity by their conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity of those who preach evangelical poverty should be tested by whether they 'throw their own goods into common, and submit their own persons to the austere discipline of the early Church.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose hypocrisy by comparing rhetorical claims to actual personal sacrifice; treat failure to practice principles as evidence of fraud or self-interest rather than authentic zeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uphold public faith and honor obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and original faith of civil society is pledged to the property of the citizen, not to the demands of the public creditor; public obligations should be limited to the public estate ('It is to the property of the citizen, and not to the demands of the creditor of the state, that the first and original faith of civil society is pledged').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on legal and moral priority of private property and pre-existing contracts; argue that creditors' security was meant to be public revenue, not individuals' estates. Use this principle to challenge measures that selectively appropriate private assets to satisfy public debt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in recognition of past acts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inconsistent to hold only pecuniary engagements of the old government valid while rejecting other acts and titles ('No acts of the old government of the kings of France are held valid ... except its pecuniary engagements').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attack selective validation as partiality and sophistry; demand coherent principles for which past acts are honored or discarded. Point out practical inequities when some titles/claims are respected and others are branded illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider economic consequences before radical redistribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass immediate sale of a vast landed estate would depress land values and divert circulating money from trade to land, defeating the aims of confiscation ('To bring this unwieldy mass of landed property ... at once into market was obviously to defeat the profits ... by depreciating the value of those lands').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use market logic and economic cause-and-effect to show that hastily liquidating large property holdings harms overall wealth and undermines intended financial remedies; propose assessing practical effects and alternatives (e.g., proportioned assessments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical analogy and classical examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ historical comparisons (Roman confiscators, Henry VIII, etc.) to illuminate contemporary actions and to show continuity of tyrannical patterns ('Few barbarous conquerors have ever made so terrible a revolution in property' ... comparisons with Roman factions and Henry VIII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select apt historical precedents to demonstrate moral lessons, cautionary parallels, and to shame or warn current actors; classical allusion strengthens authority and symmetry of the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose hypocrisy, cant, and sophistry of opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Reveal rhetorical contradiction and fraud in opponents' language and pretenses ('Their language is in the patois of fraud, in the cant and gibberish of hypocrisy' ... 'The sophistic tyrants of Paris').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace inconsistencies between claimed motives and actions; characterize dishonest rhetoric as 'patois' or 'cant' to delegitimize opponents' moral claims. Contrast words with deeds to erode their credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rouse moral emotions and national pride
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appeals to national feeling and moral horror to mobilize sympathy and alarm ('It is with the exultation of a little national pride I tell you ... It has roused the people. They see with horror and alarm ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend reasoned argument with moral diction and appeals to pride, shame, and compassion; evoke public sentiment to make the case resonate beyond abstract theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground arguments in concrete fiscal data and practical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Support claims with numerical budgets and concrete fiscal accounting (citation of Necker's budget figures: deficiency 56,150,000 livres; short of 2,200,000 l. sterling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exact figures, documented reports, and practical assessments to show alternatives to drastic measures; demonstrating feasible, proportioned solutions undercuts the necessity of radical confiscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and critique interest-group alliances behind policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Expose alliances (the moneyed interest, men of letters, a literary cabal) that direct opinion and policy for private ends ('the alliance, therefore, of these writers with the moneyed interest ... served as a link to unite ... obnoxious wealth to restless and desperate poverty').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the social and economic networks that benefit from proposed measures; show how allied groups manufacture consent and direct public indignation, thereby revealing motives and undermining policy legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend institutional checks and judicial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Warn against abolishing independent judiciary and institutions that protect citizens ('To cut off all appearance of connection between the crown and public justice, and to bring the whole under implicit obedience to the dictators in Paris, the old independent judicature of the Parliaments ... was wholly abolished').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that preserving traditional judicial bodies and legal forms prevents arbitrary power; emphasize institutions' role in allowing citizens to appeal to ancient laws and check revolutionary excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of abstract slogans used as incantations
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique the use of high-sounding abstract phrases ('Philosophy, Light, Liberality, the Rights of Men') as rhetorical incantations that paper over concrete injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn writers/readers not to accept sweeping abstractions as justification for specific, harmful policies; demand substantive reasoning and concrete evidence when abstractions are invoked.
